sources.title: SM90 (Hopper) support: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash end to end on 8x / 4x H20-3e
sources.body:
## Summary

DeepInfer currently runs on SM100 and Ascend 950. This PR adds an SM90 (Hopper) path so that DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash runs end to end on Hopper GPUs, validated on 8x and 4x NVIDIA H20-3e (141 GB):

- same checkpoint, no conversion
- attention DP / CP, MoE EP, DSpark
- CUDA graphs on

Key design points:

- The MXFP4 routed experts stay resident in FP4, so 4 GPUs are enough.
- FlashMLA's last Hopper kernels (`ba89a34`) are extended to the V4.1 KV cache formats.

SM100 and Ascend behaviour is unchanged. Every SM90 path is selected by `PLATFORM.is_sm90`, and all new kernels live in `deepinfer/model_executor/layers/sm90_ops/`.

**Results on H20-3e** (details, settings and methodology below):

| | 8x H20-3e | 4x H20-3e |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TTFT, 128K input (context parallel) | 2.15 s | 3.64 s |
| TTFT, 512K input | 9.66 s | 16.72 s |
| TTFT, ~1M input | 22.2 s | 38.5 s |
| Decode, 64 concurrent, 1024 in / 512 out, total tok/s | 3793 | 2463 |
| GSM8K (1319, 8-shot) | 0.943 | 0.941 |

TTFT: one cold request at a time, median of 3, context parallel over all GPUs, NCCL all-gather overlapped with compute. Decode: random token ids, total output tok/s. The 8-GPU run uses the default prefill intervals; the only 4-GPU run used intervals 1 / 1. GSM8K: 8-shot completion, with the first 8 test questions as shots and all 1319 scored, as in SGLang's GSM8K harness.

A comparison with SGLang on the same hardware will follow in a comment.

## What changes on SM90

| Component | SM100 | SM90 (this PR) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sparse attention, prefill and decode (V41 MXFP8 SWA cache, V41_FP4 compressed cache) | FlashMLA `2e5429f` | `flash_mla_sm90`: FlashMLA `ba89a34` (its last Hopper kernels) plus a patch that adds the V4.1 KV formats |
| FP8 linears and the `wo_a` einsum (packed UE8M0 1x32 / 32x32 scales) | DeepGEMM | block-[32, 32] FP8 Gluon GEMM, tuned for every V4.1 linear shape |
| Sparse-indexer logits (FP4 index K; dense, candidate and paged rows) | DeepGEMM `fp8_fp4` MQA logits | Triton kernels plus a Gluon keys-major prefill kernel, following the reference indexer arithmetic |
| Routed experts (MXFP4) | Mega MoE / `fp8_fp4` grouped GEMM | non-mega EP path with humming W4A8 (FP4 resident; the default when installed), or `triton_fp8` / `hybrid` / `deepgemm` |
| MoE gate, mHC | `mega_gate`, `mega_mhc` | existing `moe_topk_gate` and TileKernels mHC |
| Top-k | DeepSelect `sm_100a` | DeepSelect also built for `sm_90a`, plus a vendor patch for the 16-CTA cluster kernel H20 cannot launch |
| CP all-gather | DeepEP `BucketBuffer` (needs NVLink multicast) | by default an NCCL all-gather buffer with the same interface; `BucketBuffer` with `NCCL_NVLS_ENABLE=1` where NVLink multicast works |
| Build | — | on SM90, `./build.sh` builds `flash_mla_sm90` and installs `humming-kernels`; `scripts/vendor_patches/` holds the DeepSelect, DeepEP and FlashMLA patches |

**Footprint.** 56 files, +9140 / −72 lines.

- 25 existing files: +567 / −72. Almost all of it is gated by `is_sm90` or an explicit opt-in. The largest are `parallel_utils/cp.py` (+183 / −4) and `v4_modules/index_attn.py` (+109 / −32).
- New files:

| New files | Lines |
| --- | --- |
| SM90 kernels in `sm90_ops/` | 3280 |
| Tests | 2134 |
| `examples/`: latency benchmark, SM90 microbenchmarks | 2365 |
| Vendor patches, including the 522-line FlashMLA CUDA patch | 656 |
| Build glue: `scripts/cuda_arch.sh`, `requirements-sm90.txt` | 24 |
| `doc/sm90.md` | 113 |

- One new submodule, `vendor/FlashMLA-SM90`, pinned at `ba89a34`.

The full write-up, including build prerequisites, layouts and settings, is in [`doc/sm90.md`](doc/sm90.md).

## Commits

1. `777aec0` platform: detect Hopper (SM90) GPUs
1. `16f7e44` build: build the SM90 (Hopper) dependencies from build.sh
1. `b1f3b7d` attention: run V4.1 sparse attention on SM90
1. `12da8e7` sm90_ops: add a block-[32, 32] FP8 GEMM for Hopper
1. `23a1290` model: route FP8 linears and wo_a to the SM90 GEMM
1. `e7024f5` sm90_ops: add the sparse-indexer MQA logits for Hopper
1. `3f9631b` model: score the sparse indexer with sm90_ops on SM90
1. `c32bf07` moe: run MXFP4 routed experts on SM90
1. `f68df48` cp: fall back to NCCL all-gather without NVLS multicast
1. `d9a9bae` examples: add an offline latency benchmark
1. `b4a8287` doc: add SM90 (Hopper) setup and results

Each commit is one reviewable step and passes ruff on its own. If smaller PRs would be easier to review, I can split the series.

## Verification

**Unit tests.** On an H20-3e host, with 4 GPUs visible for the CP tests:

```bash
pytest tests/sm90 tests/models/test_sm90_moe.py tests/distributed/test_cp_manager.py
```

| Run | Result |
| --- | --- |
| The command above | 162 passed, 1 skipped |
| `pytest -m ci tests/sm90 tests/models/test_sm90_moe.py tests/benchmarks` | 20 passed |
| CPU-only collection of the same paths plus `test_cp_manager.py` | 179 tests, no errors |

The skipped test is the `BucketBuffer` half of `test_cp_manager.py`, which needs NVLink multicast that this host does not have.

The tests compare each kernel with an independent fp32 reference, or with the official reference kernels in the checkpoint's `inference/` directory:

| Component | Criterion |
| --- | --- |
| Attention | cos > 0.99999, LSE error < 1e-3 |
| FP8 GEMM | cos > 0.99999 on every V4.1 shape (bf16 outputs); cos > 0.999 for the FP8-output `wo_a` einsum |
| Indexer | matches a torch restatement of the reference math within the tests' per-logit tolerances. The FP4 → FP8 re-encoding is exact when a row's block exponents span at most 14 binades, with a documented bound beyond that |
| Routed experts | cos > 0.9999 and relative error < 2% |
| CP NCCL path | bitwise equal to a reference gather. Equal to `BucketBuffer` on a host with NVLink multicast; that comparison is skipped on hosts without it |

**Layer-level numerics.** I fed each sub-module of `inference/model.py` the same inputs DeepInfer saw at that layer, for layers 20–39 with 4K and 8K prompts:

| Sub-module | Agreement with the reference |
| --- | --- |
| Attention output | cos ≥ 0.9993 |
| MoE output | cos ≥ 0.9999 |
| Gate expert ids | 100% |
| Indexer top-k recall | 0.992–0.997 |

**End to end.**

- Greedy generation (DP8 x EP8, CUDA graphs, DSpark) answers the sample prompts correctly: Beijing, Rayleigh scattering, 72, and all 25 primes below 100. The first answer matches the reference implementation token for token.
- GSM8K: 0.943 on 8 GPUs (0.941 with DSpark off), 0.941 on 4 GPUs.

**Build from scratch.** On an 8x H20-3e host, I ran `DEEPINFER_ACCELERATOR=nvidia ./build.sh` unmodified in a clean Python 3.12 environment (`env -i`, no `CUDA_HOME`):

- It built everything in 6 min 52 s: DeepSelect, FlashMLA-SM90, DeepEP, DeepGEMM, `deepinfer._C` and `humming-kernels` 0.1.12.
- NCCL 2.32.3 is the only NCCL in the environment.
- After the build, the vendor submodules are back at their pinned commits with no local changes.
- With an R570 driver, the CUDA 13 forward-compatibility `libcuda` must be on `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`.
- In that fresh environment, with a new `HOME` and cold JIT caches, the unit tests above give 162 passed, 1 skipped. The only `libnccl` loaded is the venv's 2.32.3; no `LD_PRELOAD` or path changes are needed.

**Lint.** `ruff check --no-cache && ruff format --check --no-cache` (ruff 0.15.0) and `bash scripts/format_csrc.sh --check` pass.

**Not tested on SM100 or Ascend.** I have no such hardware. Outside the `is_sm90` branches, the diff is limited to the following. Each item keeps the existing behaviour off SM90 by construction.

- `build.sh` and `scripts/cuda_arch.sh`: every NVIDIA build now detects the GPU architecture, defaulting to sm100 when no GPU is visible. Only the sm90 result changes what is built.
- `platform.py` and `deep_cluster/hardware/{device,nvidia}.py`: a cached `is_sm90()` NVML check runs on NVIDIA GPUs. `nvidia.py` binds one more NVML symbol (`nvmlDeviceGetName`).
- `.gitmodules`: the new `vendor/FlashMLA-SM90` submodule, built only for sm90.
- `input_metadata/{dflash,input_metadata}.py`: import `FlashMLASchedMeta` through `attention_backend`, which re-exports the same class off SM90.
- `deepinfer/environ.py`: new variables only. The defaults preserve existing behaviour.
- `parallel_utils/cp.py`: off SM90, `auto` builds `BucketBuffer` exactly as before. `DEEPINFER_CP_COMM_BACKEND=nccl` is an explicit opt-in.
- `parallel_utils/userbuffer.py`: log text only.
- `examples/offline_inference.py`: on SM90 it no longer defaults `DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`. The offline decode-PPL tests skip SM90, because their goldens are SM100 batch-invariant runs.
- `scripts/build_vendor.sh`: applies `scripts/vendor_patches/` during the build and reverts the patches it applied afterwards. All current patches (DeepSelect, DeepEP, FlashMLA-SM90) apply to SM90 builds only, so SM100 and Ascend build the same sources as before.

## Performance on H20-3e

All numbers come from `examples/latency_benchmark.py`, added in this PR, with these settings:

- DSpark on: `DEEPINFER_USE_NEXTN_DECODE=5`, `DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=1`
- `DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_TRUNCATION_MODE=compact`, `DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_KEEP_TOKENS=140`
- CUDA graphs on

The TTFT prompts were code text from an earlier version of the prompt builder. The committed builder uses Python standard-library source instead, so it produces different token inputs.

**TTFT**, in seconds. One cold request at a time, median of 3 runs after 1 warm-up, prefill intervals set to 1.

The CP all-gathers use NCCL, the SM90 default. They were measured with `DEEPINFER_CP_NCCL_OVERLAP=1`, which overlaps them with compute. The default now waits for each all-gather at launch instead. With that default, a from-scratch build of this series on another 8x H20-3e host measured 0.188 s at 1K and 2.107 s at 128K.

| Input | 1K | 4K | 16K | 64K | 128K | 256K | 512K | ~1M |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 8 GPUs, CP8 | 0.189 | 0.188 | 0.308 | 1.068 | 2.146 | 4.458 | 9.662 | 22.19 |
| 4 GPUs, CP4 | 0.184 | 0.190 | 0.492 | 1.791 | 3.636 | 7.641 | 16.72 | 38.48 |
| 8 GPUs, DP8 (no CP, one GPU per request) | 0.176 | 0.364 | 1.182 | 4.568 | 9.461 | 20.22 | 46.05 | 113.1 |

**Decode**, 8 GPUs, DP8 x EP8, random token ids, 1024 in / 512 out, seed 20261018. Output tok/s, with median TPOT in parentheses. For one request the rate excludes TTFT; for 32 and 64 requests it is total throughput.

| Concurrency | Default prefill intervals (70 / 100) | Prefill intervals 1 / 1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 158 (6.34 ms) | 163 (6.13 ms) |
| 32 | 2618 (6.30 ms) | 2167 (9.63 ms) |
| 64 | 3793 (7.43 ms) | 2930 (14.13 ms) |

Why the two columns differ:

- With intervals 1 / 1, every new request starts its prefill at once. DP ranks advance in lockstep, so the other ranks run slower decode steps meanwhile.
- The default intervals batch those prefills. Under load, this cuts the median TPOT by 35–47%.
- Profiling with 4K-in / 1K-out coding prompts puts the steady-state decode step at about 33–34 ms. The gap between the columns is prefill interference, not kernel time.

**4 GPUs**, DP4 x EP4, random token ids (seed 0), 1024 in / 512 out, prefill intervals 1 / 1:

| Concurrency | Total output tok/s |
| --- | --- |
| 32 | 1981 |
| 64 | 2463 |

## Environment

| Item | Version |
| --- | --- |
| GPUs | 8x / 4x NVIDIA H20-3e (141 GB, NVLink), SM90 |
| Driver | R570 with CUDA 13 forward compatibility, and R590 |
| CUDA / PyTorch | CUDA 13.0–13.2, torch 2.13.0 |
| Vendored | DeepGEMM 1fc9c66, DeepEP 93eb6eb, DeepSelect bfa4507 (+ `scripts/vendor_patches/`), FlashMLA ba89a34 (+ V4.1 patch) |
| SM90 extras | `humming-kernels==0.1.12` (default MoE backend when installed) |
| Model | `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017`, unmodified |
| Code | Performance and accuracy numbers come from integration builds of this series, before the history was squashed into these commits; the kernels and model wiring are the same, and the CP rows used the overlapped NCCL mode (see TTFT). The unit tests and the from-scratch build ran on a release candidate. It differs from these commits only in comments, docs, test file names, the benchmark prompt builder, the SM90 default of `examples/offline_inference.py`, and patch bookkeeping in `build_vendor.sh`. |

## Reproduce

```bash
export DEEPINFER_ACCELERATOR=nvidia
./build.sh                       # detects SM90; or set DEEPINFER_CUDA_ARCH=sm90
pytest tests/sm90 tests/models/test_sm90_moe.py tests/distributed/test_cp_manager.py
python examples/offline_inference.py

export DEEPINFER_USE_NEXTN_DECODE=5 DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=1
export DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_TRUNCATION_MODE=compact DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_KEEP_TOKENS=140

# TTFT, CP8, prefill intervals 1 for single-request latency.
# DEEPINFER_CP_NCCL_OVERLAP=1 matches the measured setting; omit it for the default.
DEEPINFER_CP_NCCL_OVERLAP=1 DEEPINFER_PREFILL_ATTEMPT_INTERVAL=1 DEEPINFER_PREFILL_ANY_ATTEMPT_INTERVAL=1 \
  python examples/latency_benchmark.py --ep 8 --cp 8 --suites ttft --out_dir runs/ttft-cp8

# Decode, DP8 x EP8, random ids 1024 in / 512 out, default prefill intervals
python examples/latency_benchmark.py --ep 8 --suites single,concurrency --prompt random --seed 20261018 \
  --decode_input_len 1024 --decode_output_len 512 --concurrency 32 64 --out_dir runs/decode-dp8

# GSM8K, SGLang's shot layout: the first 8 test questions are shots, and all 1319 are scored
python examples/latency_benchmark.py --ep 8 --suites gsm8k --gsm8k_data test.jsonl --gsm8k_overlap_shots \
  --out_dir runs/gsm8k
```

## Notes for reviewers

- **Dependencies.**
  - `humming-kernels` (PyPI, Apache-2.0) is imported lazily, only on SM90 and only by the humming / hybrid MoE backends. Without it, `auto` uses the pure-Triton `triton_fp8` backend. That backend needs about twice the expert memory, so it fits at EP8 but not at EP4.
  - `flash_mla_sm90` is built from a patch on FlashMLA `ba89a34`. I am happy to send the patch to FlashMLA instead.
  - The DeepSelect and DeepEP patches (SM90 builds only) are candidates for those projects.
- **Indexer numerics.** The SM90 indexer follows the reference implementation's arithmetic, including an fp32 head sum. Its top-k picks can therefore differ from SM100 on near-ties.
- **Not ported.** The SM100-only fused kernels (Mega MoE, `mega_gate`, `mega_mhc`, candidate-sparse MQA) are not ported; SM90 uses the existing non-mega paths.
- **Known gaps.**
  - Single-request TTFT has a floor of about 0.19 s for prompts up to 8K tokens, because short prefills run eagerly and are bound by launch overhead.
  - On hosts where NVLink multicast works, setting `NCCL_NVLS_ENABLE=1` lets CP use DeepEP's `BucketBuffer`. That was 3–5% faster than the default NCCL path at long context.
- **Open PRs touching the same code.**
  - #60 (vendor registry) and #88 change `get_bf16_tflops_limit`, as this PR does. If either lands first, I will rebase.
  - `PLATFORM.is_sm90` is a capability flag on the existing GPU platform, not a new `PlatformEnum` member, in line with the direction in #63.
- **Not verified.**
  - SM100 and Ascend were not run; I have no such hardware. Those paths are unchanged by construction, apart from the items listed above.
  - Hopper parts other than H20-3e, and multi-node runs, were not tested.
- **Follow-ups.**
  - A DeepEP change that lets `BucketBuffer` all-gather without multicast. It is prototyped and bitwise-checked, but not included here.
  - A faster candidate-row indexer kernel.

## Checklist

- [x] `ruff check` / `ruff format --check` (ruff 0.15.0) and `scripts/format_csrc.sh --check` pass
- [x] New tests under `tests/`; SM90-only tests skip elsewhere
- [x] Unit, numerics and end-to-end results on SM90 hardware
- [x] SM100 / Ascend code paths unchanged (gated by `PLATFORM.is_sm90`); not run on SM100 hardware
- [x] Documentation: `doc/sm90.md`

sources.title: Add an NVLink Engram fetch for single-node runs without NCCL GIN
sources.body:
## Summary

DeepSeek-V4.1 cannot currently run on a node where **NCCL GIN (GPU-initiated RDMA) is unavailable**, even on a single node with all GPUs on NVLink. Examples:

- cloud single-node GPU instances without RDMA;
- development or lab nodes whose compute NICs are not cabled or are disabled;
- hosts whose NIC, firmware or driver setup does not support GDAKI.

This PR adds an opt-in NVLink-only path for the Engram fetch so these nodes can run the model.

## Why Engram is the blocker

`deep_ep.EngramBuffer.fetch` is implemented only on top of GIN. `engram_fetch.cuh` issues `comm::NCCLGin` gets even when `num_rdma_ranks == 1`, because the shards live in host memory owned by other ranks. Without GIN:

- by default, `EngramBuffer` creation fails with `GIN: DevComm setup failed on all available backends`;
- with `EP_DISABLE_GIN=1`, the first forward (the profile run) hits `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` in the Engram fetch kernel. DeepEP's own `tests/engram/test_engram.py` fails the same way.

Everything else in DeepInfer already works over NVLink in this setting. With `EP_DISABLE_GIN=1`, DeepEP `test_barrier.py` and `test_ep.py` (with `--allow-hybrid-mode 0`) and DeepGEMM `test_mega_moe.py` all pass.

## Changes

The default behavior is unchanged: when the flag is off, DeepEP's `EngramBuffer` is used exactly as before.

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `deepinfer/model_executor/parallel_utils/engram_nvlink.py` | **New.** `NVLinkEngramBuffer`, a drop-in for the `write` / `fetch` / `destroy` subset used by `EngramRuntime` |
| `deepinfer/environ.py` | `DEEPINFER_ENGRAM_NVLINK_FETCH`; when unset it follows `EP_DISABLE_GIN` |
| `deepinfer/model_executor/parallel_utils/userbuffer.py` | `allocate_engram()` returns `NVLinkEngramBuffer` when the flag is on |
| `deepinfer/model_executor/models/v4_modules/engram.py` | In NVLink mode, `initialize()` passes the host shards instead of CUDA views of them |
| `tests/distributed/test_engram_nvlink.py` | **New.** 2-GPU `ci` test (skipped with fewer GPUs) |

### How the fetch works

1. **`write`**
   - Each rank keeps its shard in pinned host memory and reads it through UVA. With `DEEPINFER_ENGRAM_FORCE_GPU_STORAGE`, the shard is kept on the GPU instead.
   - The full FP8 scale table is kept on the GPU, about 6 GB per rank for V4.1.
2. **`fetch`**
   - Indices are padded to `max_num_tokens` and all-gathered.
   - Each rank `index_select`s the rows it owns and zero-fills the rest.
   - One `all_to_all_single` returns the rows to the requesting ranks.
   - Each rank selects rows by owner rank.
   - Output matches DeepEP: `[T, E·H]` rows, plus scales in the TMA-aligned (4) column-major layout.
3. **No host sync.** The fetch is captured by the existing CUDA graphs.

**Trade-off:** this is a collective, not a one-sided get. Every fetch moves `max_num_tokens`-padded buffers over NVLink and needs all ranks to take part. It aims to make these nodes work, not to match GIN performance.

## Usage

```bash
export EP_DISABLE_GIN=1   # also enables DEEPINFER_ENGRAM_NVLINK_FETCH
python examples/offline_inference.py --ep 4
```

## Testing

Setup: one node, 4× B200, NVLink, GIN unavailable, driver 580.178, CUDA 13.1, torch 2.13.0+cu132, NCCL 2.32.3.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `ruff check --no-cache` / `ruff format --check --no-cache` | ✅ |
| `pytest tests/distributed/test_engram_nvlink.py` (2 GPUs) | ✅ 1 passed. FP8 rows and scales are byte-identical to a direct full-table lookup, with ragged token counts across ranks (64 / 1 / 7–8 / 32–33) and the expected scale strides |
| `examples/offline_inference.py --ep 4` before this PR (`EP_DISABLE_GIN=1`) | ❌ illegal address in the first forward |
| `examples/offline_inference.py --ep 4` **with this PR** | ✅ Completes with 50/50 samples. Profile run, KV-cache init, warm-up and CUDA graph capture all pass. Outputs are identical across DP ranks |

Note: on this host, NCCL's NVLS multicast setup intermittently fails with `Cuda failure 999` in `ncclMcGroupBuildPartitions`, independent of this change. The unit test was run with `NCCL_NVLS_ENABLE=0`.

Sample outputs (DP 0):

| # | Prompt | Output | tokens | accept | decode_ppl |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 中国的首都是哪里？ | 北京 … | 96 | 53% | 1.1832 |
| 1 | Who wrote Romeo and Juliet? | William Shakespeare … | 104 | 51% | 1.0850 |
| 2 | 1 image: carrot color | Orange … | 128 | 47% | 1.3260 |
| 3 | 3 images | Carrots … | 34 | 32% | 1.4925 |
| 4 | 5-image 4-shot | `4\n\nRelated questions` ⚠️ | 5 | 0% | 2.0001 |

## ⚠️ Open questions

- **Decode PPL does not match `tests/models/offline_decode_ppl.json`**, and sample 4's answer is wrong. The run differs from the golden setup in more than this change:
  - **Checkpoint:** local `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` (snapshot `dba1be0a`) vs the default `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017`.
  - **Parallel config:** EP4 / CP1 / DP4 vs the golden's EP4 / CP2 / DP2.
  - **This change:** Engram over NVLink. MLOPart was also unavailable on this host.

  None of these has been isolated yet. I don't have a GIN-capable node for an A/B against the native path, so a check from someone who does would be very helpful. I also plan to run GSM8K next.
- **Performance is not measured yet.** The only end-to-end run was the first one and included JIT compilation.
- **Better design?** On a single node, a one-sided alternative is possible: put the whole table in shared, `cudaHostRegister`ed host memory and read the needed rows through UVA. That avoids both the collectives and the padding. I'd welcome maintainer input on which direction you prefer.

sources.title: eplb: aggregate the expert-count window by logical expert at record time
sources.body:
## Problem

`ExpertLoadBalancer` keeps a ring buffer of per-step expert token counts (`_expert_count_window`) and hands the aggregate to `rebalance_experts_global` on every rearrangement. The window stored raw **per-local-physical-slot** counts, and `_rearrange_experts` decoded *all* entries with the `physical_to_logical_map` that is current at rearrangement time:

```python
logical_expert_token_counts.scatter_add_(
    -1,
    local_physical_to_logical_map.to(torch.int64).expand_as(self._expert_count_window),
    self._expert_count_window,
)
```

Every rearrangement re-keys the physical slots (`self.physical_to_logical_map.copy_(next_physical_to_logical_map)`), but the window was never cleared or re-keyed. Entries recorded under an earlier placement are therefore attributed to whichever logical expert now occupies the slot.

In plain interval mode this is masked: the constructor enforces `window_size <= rearrangement_interval`, so the ring is fully overwritten between rearrangements. With `DEEPINFER_REARRANGE_AFTER_PREFILL_IN_NORMAL_ENGINE=1`, however, `_update_rearrangement` forces a rearrangement on the step after **every** prefill. Under continuous batching that is far more often than `window_size` decode steps, so most of the window holds counts recorded under one or more dead placements. The second and later rearrangements then optimize a scrambled load distribution: hot experts under-replicated, cold ones replicated, placements oscillating after each prefill while paying a full all-layer weight shuffle each time. `rank_balance` / `logical_balance` in the `[EPLB] rearranged` log line are computed from the same scrambled counts, so the logs do not show it.

## Fix

Record the window as `[window_size, num_moe_layers, num_logical_experts]`: each step's slot counts are scatter-added with the placement that is current **when the step is recorded**. `_rearrange_experts` then only has to clone and all-reduce the window; the tensor handed to `rebalance_experts_global` and to `_log_rearrangement_metrics` has exactly the same shape and meaning as before, so the policy and the metrics are untouched.

The rank slice of `physical_to_logical_map` is factored into `_local_physical_to_logical_map()`; it is a view, so it tracks the in-place `copy_` after each shuffle.

Memory: the window grows from `num_local_physical_experts` to `num_logical_experts` per layer per entry (int32). For V4.1-Flash at the default window of 100 steps this is on the order of a few MB.

## Tests

`tests/models/test_eplb_window.py` (CPU-only, marked `ci` and `ci_npu`) drives `_update_rearrangement` directly with a two-method fake process group and checks that:

- an entry recorded before a placement change keeps its original attribution, and an entry recorded after it uses the new placement;
- ring wrap replaces the slot rather than accumulating into it;
- the rank slice follows `ep_group.rank()`.

Ran these tests, plus a CPU smoke run of three consecutive `_rearrange_experts` cycles through the real `rebalance_experts_global` and metrics logging with collectives stubbed. I do not have SM100 / Ascend hardware, so the GPU path was not exercised; the change does not touch the shuffle or the kernels.

sources.title: [Bugfix][DeepSeek V4] Load redundant EPLB expert slots
sources.body:
## Overview

Fixes #59609. With `--enable-eplb` and `num_redundant_experts > 0`, DeepSeek V4 and V4.1 never loaded the redundant expert slots. `get_expert_mapping` now passes `num_redundant_experts`, so `load_weights` fills those slots.

Scope: NVIDIA only. Only the NVIDIA V4 and V4.1 models allocate redundant expert slots; on ROCm, V4 builds its MoE layers without EPLB and V4.1 sets `n_redundant_experts = 0`.

## Claims

- On the FusedMoE path (every `--moe-backend` except `deep_gemm_mega_moe`, which already loads the replicas), redundant EPLB slots hold the weights of the logical expert they replicate. Before this change they kept uninitialized memory.
- No change when `num_redundant_experts=0`.

## Validation

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on 4x B300, TP=4, `--enable-expert-parallel --enable-eplb`, default `--moe-backend auto` (FLASHINFER_TRTLLM_MXFP4_MXFP8), `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`, `--max-model-len 8192`. "Replica slots that differ" compares a checksum of every redundant slot's EPLB-managed weights against the slot holding the same logical expert (8 slots x 40 MoE layers). GSM8K: 250 test questions, 5-shot, greedy.

| Config | Replica slots that differ | GSM8K |
| --- | --- | --- |
| N=0, main | no replicas | 88.8% (222/250) |
| N=8, main | 320 / 320 (all zero bytes) | 88.8% (222/250) |
| N=8, this PR | 0 / 320 | 88.0% (220/250) |

GSM8K is not sensitive to this bug: only 8 of 384 experts have a replica, and only the tokens routed to the replica lose that expert's output. Short greedy prompts show it more directly. On main with N=8, "Explain in two sentences why the sky is blue." ends at end-of-sequence as its first token (logprob -1.13 vs -1.63 for the runner-up). With this PR, " The" wins (-1.77) and end-of-sequence is second (-2.27).

The reproducer in #59609 prints `redundant slots with all-zero weights: 320 / 320` on main and `redundant slots with all-zero weights: 0 / 320` with this PR.

The new e2e test (below) fails on main and passes with this PR, run locally on 4x B300 with DeepSeek-V4-Flash:

| | Startup weight check | GSM8K (1319 q) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| main | `344 redundant expert slots differ from their source` (8 x 43 layers) | not reached |
| this PR | passes on all 4 ranks | 94.8% |

```
cd tests && PYTHONPATH=.. pytest -s -v evals/gsm8k/test_gsm8k_correctness.py --config-list-file=configs/models-spec-decode.txt -k EPLB
```

## Details

`DeepseekV4Model.load_weights` loads routed experts only through the ids returned by `get_expert_mapping`. That mapping was built with the default `num_redundant_experts=0`, so physical ids `n_routed_experts..n_routed_experts+N-1` were never passed to the weight loader. EPLB's initial placement maps those slots to logical experts `0..N-1` and sends part of those experts' tokens to them.

DeepseekV2 has the same missing argument in `get_expert_mapping` (#41920, #41930). There, `load_weights` builds its own mapping with redundant slots, so only BitsAndBytes and LoRA are affected. In V4 and V4.1, `load_weights` uses `get_expert_mapping` directly, so the slots are never loaded.

Not changed:
- `deep_gemm_mega_moe` uses `make_deepseek_v4_expert_params_mapping`, which is a separate path.
- The ROCm V4.1 model sets `n_redundant_experts = 0`.
- The MTP loader (`deepseek_v4/nvidia/mtp.py`) builds its mapping without redundant slots too. The drafter is not registered with EPLB, so its router never selects those slots. This is inferred from the code, not tested.

Test: the GSM8K harness gets an optional `startup_rpc_checks` config key. It calls each listed worker-extension method through `/collective_rpc` after the server starts and before any request. The check runs before traffic because EPLB rearrangement can move expert weights. `tests/evals/gsm8k/eplb_checks.py` checksums every expert slot, gathers the checksums across the EP group, and compares each redundant slot with the first slot of the same logical expert. GSM8K alone does not catch this bug: on V4.1-Flash it scored 88.8% on main and 88.0% with the fix. The new `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-EPLB-TEP4.yaml` (TP4, EP, 8 redundant experts) runs in the nightly ":nvidia: (B200) LM Eval Spec Decode" job. The check takes a few seconds; the config adds one V4-Flash cold start plus about a minute of GSM8K to that job.

---

sources.title: [Perf][Kernel] Add a CuteDSL BF16x3 router GEMM for fp32 router weights on Hopper
sources.body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

On H100/H200, `GateLinear` runs fp32 router weights above 32 tokens as `F.linear(x.float(), w)`, an fp32 SGEMM on CUDA cores. SM100 has the CuteDSL BF16x3 kernel for this (#47973, #55899) and gfx950 has a hipBLASLt one (#52668). SM90 had nothing. This PR adds a CuteDSL BF16x3 kernel for SM90 behind the existing BF16x3 tier.

Models on main that hit this path on SM90 (fp32 router weight, bf16 activations): MiniMax-M2/M2.5/M3, GLM-4.5/4.6/4.7 and GLM-4.5-Air, Hunyuan-V3/V4, Step-3.5-Flash, ERNIE-4.5, Ling 2.0 (`router_dtype: fp32`), and others. The new models are on it too. Beam-1.0 (#62074) keeps fp32 router weights `(5120, 256)`, and Muse Spark Open (#61879) keeps `(8192, 256)`. Both shapes are in the fp32 GEMV table since #62042 and #62126, so on H200 every batch above its limit runs the fp32 SGEMM.

The first revision of this PR used Triton. It is now CuteDSL, like the other router GEMMs in the tree, and uses the `VllmJitKernel` warmup contract.

## Claims

- Router GEMM on 1xH200, inside CUDA graphs with cold L2, over 10 router shapes: 1.6-3.8x faster at 33-512 tokens and 3.3-7.7x faster at 1024-16384 tokens.
- MAE against an fp64 reference is 0.16-0.73x that of the fp32 SGEMM it replaces, at every shape and token count measured.
- MiniMax-M2.5 FP8, TP2 on 2xH200, with main and PR alternating in one container: TTFT 3-5% lower for 8K and 32K prompts, prefill throughput 4-6% higher, and on a mixed 1K-in/128-out workload 4.6% more output tokens/s and 4% lower TPOT. GSM8K accuracy is unchanged and its wall time is 2.5% lower.
- In eager mode one router call costs 17-18 µs of host time, against 21-36 µs on main.
- Beam-1.0 FP8 on one H200, as one TP8 rank (all 52 layers, dummy weights, main and PR alternating): an 8K prefill chunk takes 14.0% less time (155.3 to 133.5 ms), and a decode step at 64 and 128 requests takes 7.4% and 10.9% less.
- On SM90 the fp32 GEMV now runs up to 24 tokens instead of 32, where the new kernel is faster. The GB200 rule for `(5120, 256)` from #62042 stays Blackwell-only.
- No change for 24 or fewer tokens on the fp32 GEMV shapes, under `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT`, or on other architectures.

## Validation

### Unit tests

The new test checks that the MAE against fp64 is not above the fp32 SGEMM's for 9 router shapes (now with Beam-1.0 and Muse Spark Open) and 12 token counts (8 to 8192). It also checks:
- partial K and expert tiles, and a K with fewer tiles than the largest split;
- that the weight split is bit-exact (one-hot activations);
- CUDA graph replay and strided activations;
- that warmup compiles from fake tensors every key the runtime then uses;
- `GateLinear`: the kernel runs above 24 tokens for fp32-GEMV shapes (including 32 and 48 tokens for `(5120, 256)`) and for a generic shape, the fp32 GEMV still runs at 1, 16 and 24 tokens for all 5 fp32-GEMV shapes, the warmup is registered, and `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT` turns the tier off.

It runs in the `(H100) BF16x3 Router GEMM Kernels` Buildkite step. The B200 catch-all ignores it, as for #52668.

```python
print("device", torch.cuda.get_device_name(), "torch", torch.__version__, flush=True)

SHAPES = {

}

SCALE = 0.053


def graph_time_us(fns, reps=7):

        f()

    g = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
    with torch.cuda.graph(g):
        for f in fns:

    g.replay()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    times = []
    for _ in range(reps):
        s = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        t = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        s.record()
        g.replay()
        t.record()
        t.synchronize()
        times.append(s.elapsed_time(t) * 1000 / len(fns))
    return statistics.median(times)


def mae(out, ref):
    return (out.double() - ref).abs().mean().item()


def main_path(x, w):
    return torch.nn.functional.linear(x.float(), w)


def pr_path(x, w):
    return torch.ops.vllm.sm90_bf16x3_router_gemm(x, w)


rows = []
for name, (k, e) in SHAPES.items():
    gen = torch.Generator(device=dev).manual_seed(0)
    for m in MS:
        nc = int(min(64, max(4, -(-4 * L2_BYTES // (m * k * 2 + e * k * 4)))))
        xs = [torch.randn(m, k, generator=gen, device=dev).to(torch.bfloat16) for _ in range(nc)]
        ws = [torch.randn(e, k, generator=gen, device=dev) * SCALE for _ in range(nc)]
        ref = xs[0].double() @ ws[0].double().T
        row = {"model": name, "K": k, "E": e, "M": m}
        for label, fn in (("main", main_path), ("pr", pr_path)):
            row[f"{label}_us"] = round(graph_time_us([lambda i=i: fn(xs[i], ws[i]) for i in range(nc)]), 2)
            row[f"{label}_mae"] = mae(fn(xs[0], ws[0]), ref)
        row["speedup"] = round(row["main_us"] / row["pr_us"], 2)
        rows.append(row)
        print(json.dumps(row), flush=True)
        del xs, ws
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()

os.makedirs("control/artifacts", exist_ok=True)
with open("control/artifacts/pr_component.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump({"device": torch.cuda.get_device_name(), "torch": torch.__version__, "rows": rows}, f, indent=1)
```

</details>

### SM90 cutoff for the fp32 GEMV (1xH200)

Same timing method, per call in µs, fp32 GEMV / this kernel. The new kernel is almost flat up to 96 tokens. The fp32 GEMV grows with the token count.

| (K, E) | M=16 | M=24 | M=25 | M=32 | M=40 | M=48 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Beam-1.0 (5120, 256) | 5.79 / 7.52 | 7.47 / 7.52 | 7.58 / 7.53 | 9.70 / 7.56 | 11.86 / 7.62 | 13.82 / 7.59 |
| Muse Spark Open (8192, 256) | 7.80 / 9.87 | 10.79 / 9.91 | 11.12 / 9.93 | 14.11 / 9.97 | - | - |
| Step-5 (4096, 352) | 6.38 / 6.87 | 8.42 / 6.92 | 8.80 / 6.92 | 8.59 / 6.91 | - | - |
| MiniMax-M2/M2.5 (3072, 256) | 4.09 / 5.94 | 4.99 / 5.93 | 5.19 / 5.96 | 6.97 / 5.94 | - | - |
| MiniMax-M3 (6144, 128) | 5.78 / 8.07 | 8.05 / 8.10 | 8.02 / 8.10 | 10.36 / 8.11 | - | - |

The crossover is at 18-28 tokens depending on the shape. With 24 for all shapes, each shape stays within 1.5 µs of the faster kernel. The GB200 rule from #62042 (fp32 GEMV up to 48 tokens for multiples of 8, else 16) would cost up to 6.2 µs per call here (48 tokens: 13.82 vs 7.59), so it now applies only on Blackwell. Two rounds; the spread is within 0.2 µs.

At 25-32 tokens the new kernel's MAE is 0.89-1.15x the fp32 GEMV's (for example Beam at 25 tokens: 4.2e-7 vs 4.1e-7), and well below the fp32 SGEMM's that main runs from 33 tokens. Neither kernel picks a different top-8 than fp64 at any measured point; the fp32 SGEMM does in 1 of 16384 rows for Beam-1.0 and MiniMax-M3.

### Beam-1.0 FP8, one TP8 rank on 1xH200

#62074 is not merged, so this runs its model code on top of this branch. The model is one TP8 rank of Beam-1.0 FP8: all 52 layers and 256 experts, so the router is the real `(5120, 256)` fp32 GEMM; attention heads and MLP widths are one rank's share (6 Q heads, 1 KV head, expert width 320). Weights are dummy, with `--moe-backend triton` and `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` as in the H200 recipe. There is no all-reduce. The main arm keeps this branch but turns the SM90 tier off in `GateLinear`, which is what main runs. Arms ran in one container in the order main, PR, PR, main, 3 runs each. The PR arm was the merge commit before the 24-token cutoff; no step here has 25-48 router rows.

| | main | PR | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8K prefill chunk (ms) | 155.08-155.57 | 133.39-133.99 | -14.0% |
| 64 x 512-token prompts, prefill (s) | 0.626-0.627 | 0.538-0.542 | -14.0% |
| Decode step, 64 requests (ms) | 8.120-8.133 | 7.519-7.528 | -7.4% |
| Decode step, 128 requests (ms) | 9.377-9.385 | 8.360-8.378 | -10.9% |

The savings match the kernel numbers. At 8192 tokens one router call drops by 432 µs, and 49 MoE layers give 21.2 ms per chunk; measured is 21.8 ms. At 128 tokens it is 19.3 µs x 49 = 0.95 ms per step; measured is 1.02 ms. On a real TP8 deployment every rank still runs the full router, so the time saved per step is the same, but the step also includes all-reduce, so the relative gain will be smaller than here.

### End-to-end: MiniMax-M2.5 FP8, TP2, 2xH200

`vllm serve MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2.5 --tensor-parallel-size 2 --trust-remote-code --max-model-len 40960 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 --no-enable-prefix-caching --jit-monitor-mode warn --jit-monitor-verbose`, with the default 8192 batched tokens and CUDA graphs. All runs were in one container, in the order main, PR, main, PR. Before each arm, its files were copied over the installed package and the server was restarted, with `VLLM_DISABLE_COMPILE_CACHE=1`. Each `vllm bench serve --dataset-name random --random-range-ratio 0 --ignore-eos` workload ran twice per arm, so 4 runs per side.

| Workload | main (4 runs) | PR (4 runs) | Change of the means |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8K prompt, 1 at a time: median TTFT (ms) | 328 / 332 / 332 / 331 | 317 / 318 / 314 / 313 | -4.6% |
| 32K prompt, 1 at a time: median TTFT (ms) | 1808 / 1812 / 1812 / 1816 | 1761 / 1757 / 1746 / 1750 | -3.2% |
| 8K prompts, concurrency 16: req/s | 3.56 / 3.56 / 3.57 / 3.56 | 3.77 / 3.77 / 3.78 / 3.77 | +5.8% |
| 32K prompts, concurrency 4: req/s | 0.601 / 0.602 / 0.602 / 0.601 | 0.625 / 0.625 / 0.625 / 0.625 | +3.9% |
| 1K in / 128 out, concurrency 64: output tok/s | 1422 / 1472 / 1461 / 1467 | 1518 / 1525 / 1523 / 1522 | +4.6% |
| same: mean TPOT (ms) | 39.0 / 37.8 / 38.1 / 38.0 | 36.8 / 36.7 / 36.6 / 36.7 | -4.0% |

The prefill rows are GPU-bound 8K chunks, so the router speedup shows directly (62 layers). Decode at 32 or fewer requests is unchanged by design.

GSM8K (`tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py`, 1319 questions, 5-shot, concurrency 128), twice per arm:

| | main | PR |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | 0.9287 / 0.9378 / 0.9333 / 0.9310 (mean 0.9327) | 0.9356 / 0.9340 / 0.9303 / 0.9356 (mean 0.9339) |
| Wall time (s) | 94.9 / 92.0 / 90.9 / 90.3 | 90.4 / 92.4 / 88.1 / 88.0 |

GSM8K at concurrency 128 mostly runs mixed steps above the CUDA graph sizes, so they run eagerly. With the Triton revision its wall time was slower than main in 3 of 4 containers, from the host time per router call. This version takes less host time per call than main (see Host overhead).

## Details

**Kernel.** The MMA runs swapped: 64 experts form the wgmma M dimension and tokens the N dimension (32 to 128 per CTA), so small batches still fill the instruction. One TMA warp brings fp32 weight tiles and bf16 token tiles into shared memory. The MMA warpgroup reads each k16 slice of its weight fragment as fp32 and splits it in registers into three bf16 terms. Each term keeps the top 16 bits of what is left, so the three terms sum back to the weight bit for bit. It then issues register-A wgmma against the token tile, and splits the next slice while the current one runs. Products with bf16 activations are exact in fp32, so all error comes from accumulation:
- The first-term products go to a tensor-core partial that starts from zero every K-tile (64 or 128 wide). It is then added into an fp32 register accumulator.
- The second and third terms are about 2^-8 of the output. They keep their own partial across K, as the SM100 kernel does. This is the one numerical change from the Triton revision, which promoted all three terms every K-tile. It makes the largest tiles up to 9% faster. The worst MAE in my checks is 0.87x of the fp32 SGEMM's (GLM-4.7 shape, 7 tokens).

Split-K uses a thread-block cluster of up to 8 CTAs. Each CTA writes its partial tile to its own shared memory, reusing the weight stages, and after a cluster barrier sums one slice of the tile over all peers through DSMEM, in rank order. Results are deterministic, and there is no workspace and no second kernel. There is no host sync and no data-dependent shape, so the op is safe to capture in CUDA graphs.

**Configs.** There is no autotuning. `_pick_config` scores 4 tiles x 4 splits with a fixed cost model: waves times per-CTA time. A wave is one CTA per SM, and clusters of 4 or 8 only fill 15/16 of the SMs (120 of 132; at one CTA per SM, `cuOccupancyMaxActiveClusters` gives 30 clusters of 4 and 15 of 8 on H200). The per-tile costs were fitted to H200 timings. Over 10 shapes and 14 token counts, the rule is within 0.1% (geomean) of the fastest of the 16 configs per cell, and at most 4% slower. Each of the 10 shapes reaches 9-13 configs between 1 and 16384 tokens, at about 1 s of compile each.

**Warmup.** The kernel is a `VllmCuTeDSLJitKernel`. `GateLinear` registers it with its `(K, E)` and `max_num_batched_tokens`, as it does for `ll_fp32w` and as #50177 does for SM100. Warmup traces `dispatch` over 1..max tokens and compiles each key from fake tensors, with no launch. In the end-to-end runs above, the PR arm warmed 13 keys in about 10.5 s at startup. The JIT monitor logged no compile of this kernel while serving; it logged two `fused_moe_kernel` Triton compiles on both arms.

**Host overhead.** Outside CUDA graphs (mixed prefill/decode batches above the capture sizes), the host cost per call matters as much as the kernel. `_pick_config` is cached, and the launch is one TVM-FFI call. Eager host time per call on an idle H200 host:

| | M=64 | M=930 | M=4096 |
|---|---|---|---|
| main, fp32-GEMV dispatch op (MiniMax-M2.5 shape) | 26.3 µs | 29.2 µs | 28.9 µs |
| PR, same op | 18.1 µs | 18.4 µs | 18.3 µs |
| main, `F.linear(x.float(), w)` (GLM-4.7 shape) | 21.7 µs | 24.1 µs | 36.3 µs |
| PR, `torch.ops.vllm.sm90_bf16x3_router_gemm` | 17.1 µs | 17.5 µs | 17.1 µs |

The Triton revision took about 31 µs here. Its GSM8K runs (mostly eager mixed steps) were slower than main by a few percent in some containers.

**Integration.**
- `allow_bf16x3_router_gemm` is now also true on SM90, with the same `K % 8 == 0` condition as SM100. `bf16x3_router_gemm_module()` returns the SM90 module on SM90 and the SM100 module otherwise. The fp32-GEMV dispatch op and tier 4 use it.
- In the fp32-GEMV dispatch op, SM90 bf16 inputs use the fp32 GEMV up to 24 tokens. The `(5120, 256)` GB200 rule from #62042 moved into the non-SM90 branch unchanged.
- The kernel is the custom op `torch.ops.vllm.sm90_bf16x3_router_gemm`, as #55899 does for SM100. The fp32-GEMV shapes keep dispatching on the runtime token count inside `fp32_router_gemm_dispatch`.
- PDL is on where the platform supports it, as for SM100.

**Alternatives measured on H200.**
- The Triton revision of this PR. This kernel is 1.25x faster (geomean over 10 shapes and 15 token counts). It is slower only for ERNIE-4.5 (E=64) at 128 or fewer tokens, where 9.6 µs vs 7.2 µs: one 64-expert tile and at most 8 splits leave most SMs idle. It is still 1.55x faster than main there.
- One cuBLAS GEMM over the stacked `(3E, K)` bf16 weight, which is what gfx950 does: MAE 1.4e-6 to 4.3e-6 for the Step-5 shape, worse than the fp32 SGEMM's 3-5e-7.
- A pre-split weight kept in memory: needs 1.5x the fp32 router weight per layer (about 760 MB per rank for 88 layers of Step-5). The in-register split needs no extra memory.
- One promoted partial for all three terms per k16 slice, instead of keeping the small terms apart: MAE rose above the fp32 SGEMM's at 33 tokens.
- Two MMA warpgroups per CTA, along the experts or along the tokens (up to 4): not faster than the selected configs in my sweeps.

**Limitations.**
- With one token, cuBLAS's fp32 GEMV is more accurate than this kernel for 3 of the 10 shapes (for example MiniMax-M3: MAE 3.1e-7 vs 4.7e-7). From 2 tokens up, all 10 shapes beat it. In eager mode those batches stay on the fp32 GEMV or `ll_fp32w`. The test starts at 8 tokens.
- As on SM100, generic shapes reach tier 4 through tier 3's Python check on `x.shape[0]`. Under vLLM's guard-free `torch.compile`, that branch can be fixed at the first traced size, the issue #60681 fixes for tier 1. Small batches of those shapes may then run this kernel, which is still faster than the `F.linear` path main would freeze.
- The cost model was fitted on H200 (132 SMs). Other SM90 parts get correct results and an SM-count-aware choice, but the choice may not be the fastest.
- #61727 lowers the fp32 GEMV cutoff for Step-5 to 11 tokens when `allow_bf16x3_router_gemm` is set, based on B300. On H200 the fp32 GEMV is still faster at 16 tokens for that shape, so that rule belongs in the non-SM90 branch next to the GB200 one.
- The Beam-1.0 numbers come from a one-rank proxy with dummy weights. A full TP8 run needs #62074 merged and 8xH200.

**Not a duplicate.** I listed every open PR that touches `gate_linear.py`, `fused_moe/router/`, `fp32_router_gemm*` or `ll_fp32w*`, or that has router/gate/bf16x3 in its title. Most are for other hardware or other tiers: #60376 (SM100 large batch), #60681 (tier 1 custom op), #61727 (Step-5), #50177 and #49627 (warmup), #50535, #61687, #61895, #59023 and #57626 (ROCm), #59486 (quantization), #59925 (deterministic MoE), #37306 (Llama4), #57848 (SM103) and #61463 (ll_bf16 split-K fix).

Merged since this PR opened: #62042 (`(5120, 256)` fp32 GEMV up to 48 tokens and its GB200 rule) and #62126 (Step-5 and Muse Spark Open shapes in the fp32 GEMV). Neither adds an SM90 path above the GEMV's limit. I merged main into this branch and moved the GB200 rule behind the SM90 check.

#49312 (for #49277) also targets SM90 fp32 router weights. It adds an opt-in path (`VLLM_ENABLE_HPC_ROUTER_GEMM=1`) through the external hpc-ops library, with a cached bf16 high/low copy of the weight. This PR is on by default, adds no dependency, keeps no extra weight copy, and its error stays below the fp32 SGEMM's.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to write the kernel and tests, run the benchmarks above and draft this description.

sources.title: [Fix] [NVIDIA] deepseek-v4.1: Fix the breakable prefill CUDA graph in the late-layer tail on SM90
sources.body:
## Motivation

On H200 (SM90), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with decoder SWA bounded replay (on by default; the [cookbook](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/76560713092795ac051d0411574c3a8d73145c2f/docs/cookbook/autoregressive/DeepSeek/DeepSeek-V4_1.mdx#L108) lists breakable prefill as supported with it) cannot serve with `--cuda-graph-backend-prefill breakable`. The late-layer tail fails in two places, both on paths that SM100 does not take: SM90 has no in-graph low-ratio path (`low_ratio_prefill_graph` is false), so the ratio-1/2 sources run as eager breaks or, in one place, get captured.

1. **Warmup before capture.** The first faulting kernel is the device-side assert in `torch.repeat_interleave` (`Repeat.cu:20: result_size == cumsum_ptr[size - 1]`); the CUDA 719 and DeepGEMM errors that follow are knock-on errors. Call chain: `bcg_deepseek_v4_low_ratio_sources` → `forward_low_ratio_sources` → `token_req_indices` → `repeat_interleave(req, extend_seq_lens, output_size=positions.shape[0])`. Inside the tail, the eager break sees only the tail's live rows, while `forward_batch.extend_seq_lens` still spans the whole extend. The hoisted `low_ratio_req_indices` / `low_ratio_pos_i64` already hold the tail's rows (live rows first, bucket-sized), but they are only used when their length equals the break's row count, which it does not inside an eager break.
2. **Replay of the first real request.** With (1) fixed, capture and startup succeed, and the first real prefill asserts in a replayed graph: `the output_size argument (8) must be the same as the sum of the elements in the repeats tensor (6)`. The source-layer KV write at the start of the tail (`write_tail_source_kv`) is called directly from the model, not through an eager break, so on SM90 its `token_req_indices` and the host-side compressor are captured with the capture-time row count.

#45381 fixes a different capture failure of the same low-ratio prefill-graph path on SM12x.

## Modifications

- `deepseek_v4_backend.py` (`forward_low_ratio_sources`): when the hoisted rows are longer than the break's rows in an extend, take their live prefix instead of rebuilding the rows from `extend_seq_lens`. Bucket-sized calls (the in-graph path) and calls without hoisted rows are unchanged.
  - The hoisted rows are longer only under the prefill graph, where both the prefill-graph metadata and the tail metadata store the live rows first and the padding after them. Outside the tail the live prefix therefore equals what `token_req_indices` computes; inside the tail it is the only correct value. The prefill-graph full top-k break (`_prefill_graph_full_topk_break`) already takes `low_ratio_req_indices[:real]` the same way. If a narrower condition is preferred, it can check the tail metadata explicitly; I will test that variant as well.
- `deepseek_v4.py`: a new eager break, `bcg_deepseek_v4_write_tail_source_kv`, slices the source-layer input to the live rows like `deepseek_v4_low_ratio_sources`, with the same capture-stub contract as `_low_ratio_sources_capture_stub`. The tail's source-KV write uses it inside a breakable prefill graph when the backend has no in-graph low-ratio path; every other configuration keeps the direct call. The condition reads `low_ratio_prefill_graph` the same way as the existing low-ratio call site in `_forward_prepare`. With no live rows it skips the write but still sets `tail_source_kv_layer_id`, as `write_tail_source_kv` does, so the source layer's own pass inside the tail keeps skipping its compressor.
- Tests:
  - `TestDSV4LateLayerTailLowRatioRows` checks that a tail-sized eager break gets the live prefix of the hoisted rows for both the compressor and the indexer.
  - `TestDSV4WriteTailSourceKvBreak` checks that the source-KV break passes only the first `global_num_token_non_padded_cpu` rows of `x` and `positions` to `write_tail_source_kv`, and that with zero live rows it does not call it but still marks the source layer.

  Their run is pending (the test module imports the CUDA backend and the model): I will run them on a GPU host and add the result here. `TestDSV4LateLayerTailLowRatioRows` should fail before this change (the rows rebuilt from `extend_seq_lens` do not match the break's row count) and pass after; `TestDSV4WriteTailSourceKvBreak` covers a function this PR adds, so it has no before/after comparison and only needs to pass.

## Accuracy Tests

Setup: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on 8×H200, image `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-cu13-20261018-b234b5c3`. On that image the four touched functions (`forward_low_ratio_sources`, `write_tail_source_kv`, `enter_late_layer_tail`, `prefill_graph_enter_late_layer_tail`) match `main` @ `76560713` except for the in-graph two-level branch added by #43733, which SM90 does not take. The capture stub on the new break was added while rebasing onto `main`, which gave the low-ratio break the same stub in the meantime; the measurements below predate it. I will re-run startup, smoke and accuracy on a nightly built from current `main` and update this PR, which stays a draft until then.

Launch flags: `--tp 8 --attention-backend dsv4 --moe-runner-backend marlin --mem-fraction-static 0.70 --chunked-prefill-size 16384 --prefill-decode-interval 16 --enable-decoder-swa-bounded-replay --swa-prefix-tails 1024 --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-dspark-block-size 5 --speculative-num-steps 1 --speculative-eagle-topk 1 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 6 --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 2 --language-model-only`, plus `--cuda-graph-backend-prefill breakable --cuda-graph-max-bs-prefill 4096` for the graph runs. "Eager" is the same launch without the two prefill-graph flags.

| | eager (no prefill graph) | breakable, before this change | breakable, this change |
|---|---|---|---|
| startup | ready | crashes during warmup before capture (item 1) | ready |
| first real prefill | OK | (with only the first fix: assert on replay, item 2) | OK |
| GSM8K, 1,319 questions, 5-shot, flexible / strict (lm-eval with the InferenceX setup; sgl-eval re-run pending) | 0.9727 / 0.9735 | — | 0.9727 / 0.9735 |
| long-context retrieval, 6 prompts | 6/6 | — | 6/6 |
| `max_total_num_tokens` | 23,904,000 | — | 23,904,000 |

- A second pair, measured in the same session with `--max-running-requests 64`: GSM8K 0.9742 with this change and 0.9742 eager.
- Which requests exercise the changed path: under decoder SWA bounded replay every prefill extend runs the late layers over each request's last min(extend length, 128) rows, 128 being the model's sliding window (`SWA_WINDOW`), unless it asks for prompt logprobs or every hidden state; speculative verify extends do not run the tail. (`--swa-prefix-tails 1024` is unrelated: it sizes how many radix-cached prefix tails the SWA KV pool keeps room for.) So every GSM8K and long-context prefill enters the tail, and the ones whose batch fits the captured buckets (here up to 4,096 tokens and a 16K context) run the two eager breaks changed here. Counts from the server logs are pending.
- Smoke: 15 real prefills from 1 to 30,000 words (9 single, 6 concurrent, covering the padded bucket sizes) all returned HTTP 200; server logs had no assert and no CUDA error.
- Prompt logprobs (21 fixed prompts, 40 to 12,000 words, 76,144 prompt tokens, `/generate` with `return_logprob` and `logprob_start_len 0`, T=0): the graph-vs-eager difference (mean |Δlogprob| 0.158 / 0.160) is the same as the run-to-run difference of each configuration (0.159 eager, 0.157 graph). Requests for prompt logprobs run the late layers over the whole prompt rather than the bounded tail, so this check covers the graph's numerics but not the tail path changed here; the tail path is covered by the accuracy rows and the smoke above.

`--cuda-graph-max-bs-prefill 4096`: with the default capture sizes the graph pool takes about 29.6 GB at `--mem-fraction-static 0.70`, and the first eager chunk of a 128K cold prefill (chunks past the 16K replay limit run eager) ran out of memory in the eager torch indexer scoring. Capping the capture at 4,096 tokens keeps the pool at 8.75 GB with the same KV pool size. That is a memory-headroom setting for this configuration, not part of the fix: with the default capture sizes the fix also captures, starts and serves the same smoke prefills without errors, with the same KV pool size, long-context retrieval 6/6 and GSM8K 0.9697 (within the ±0.0047 standard error); only the 128K cold prefill ran out of memory.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Cold-prefill TTFT (random-word prompts, no cache hit, `max_tokens` 1, median of 3; the nominal sizes are estimated at 2.3 words per token, so actual token counts are somewhat larger):

| 2K | 0.201 s | 0.150 s |
