Expected Number of Correct Tokens l⁡(s)l(s)




The expected number of correct tokens l⁡(s)l(s) represents how accurately the SSM can mimic the behavior of the LLM. While it is hard to directly model it with a closed form, we did an empirical measurement to observe how it scales with ss.We sampled n=200n=200 prompts as inputs and let the SSM generate m=80m=80 tokens for each prompt. The generated tokens are verified by LLM and the numbers of correct tokens are recorded. We denote the number of correct tokens generated for the ii-th prompt as lil_{i}. For an s≤80s\leq 80, we can use lil_{i}-s to approximate l⁡(s)l(s), the average number of correct tokens in the first ss tokens, as follows:




l⁡(s)≈1n​∑i=1nmin⁡{li,s}l(s)\approx\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min\left\{l_{i},s\right\}

(4)


The measured l⁡(s)l(s) curve is shown in the blue curve in Figure 2. We can use a power function




l⁡(s)≈c⋅sγl(s)\approx c\cdot s^{\gamma}

(5)


to approximate it. In this case, the approximation function is 0.9​s0.5480.9s^{0.548}, which is plotted as the orange curve.




This is also consistent with the intuition that l⁡(s)l(s) is a non-decreasing and sub-linear function (γ\gamma is always smaller than 1).
This is because we can decompose l⁡(s)l(s) as following:




l⁡(s)=∑i=1sp⁡(⋀j=1iEi)l(s)=\sum_{i=1}^{s}p(\bigwedge_{j=1}^{i}E_{i})

(6)


where pp means probability and EjE_{j} is the random event that the jj-th token is correct. Every term in the summation is non-negative. As ss increases, it is harder to make correct speculation, so the probability pp will decrease rapidly.


Figure 2: How l⁡(s)l(s) scales with ss, which can be approximated by a sublinear power function c⋅sγc\cdot s^{\gamma}, where γ<1\gamma<1. The orange curve is an approximation
0.9​s0.5480.9s^{0.548}.





LLM Runtime for Each Speculation Step tL​(b,s)t_{L}(b,s)




The runtime of one verification step of LLM tL​(b,s)t_{L}(b,s) depends on the hardware and model implementations. To illustrate how it scales with ss,
we measured the runtime of OPT-6.7B on an RTX 3090 GPU, and the result is shown in Figure 3. The runtime curves are approximately step functions. The first jump of the curve of b=1b=1 is when s=64s=64, while that of B=8B=8 jumps up much earlier when s=8s=8. For simplicity, we approximate tL​(b,s)t_{L}(b,s) as linear functions with different slopes tL​(b,s)=αb​s+βt_{L}(b,s)=\alpha_{b}s+\beta.


Figure 3: Execution time tL​(B,s)t_{L}(B,s) achieved when varying the speculation length ss for different batch sizes BB-s, which can be approximated by a linear function. 



3.3.2 SSM Runtime TST_{S}




In practice, we usually also need to consider the second term, i.e. the runtime of the small model. For a fixed BB, tS​(B,2)t_{S}(B,2) is a constant, and the constant is also increasing with respect to BB.



3.3.3 Optimal Speculation Length so​p​ts_{opt}




Based on the aforementioned analysis, the total runtime can be written as




t\displaystyle t
=N⋅tL​(b,s)l⁡(s)+1+N⋅s⋅tS​(b,1)l⁡(s)+1\displaystyle=\frac{N\cdot t_{L}(b,s)}{l(s)+1}+\frac{N\cdot s\cdot t_{S}(b,1)}{l(s)+1}

(7)



≈N​αb⋅s+β+tS​(b,1)⋅sc⋅sγ+1\displaystyle\approx N\frac{\alpha_{b}\cdot s+\beta+t_{S}(b,1)\cdot s}{c\cdot s^{\gamma}+1}

(8)


Since tS​(b,1)t_{S}(b,1) is a constant regarding ss, and is also increasing with bb as αb\alpha_{b}, we merge it with αb\alpha_{b} for simplicity.




The minimum point of this function so​p​ts_{opt} is where the derivative of tt is zero, i.e. ∂t∂s=0\frac{\partial t}{\partial s}=0. And we have




∂t∂s=N​αb​(c⋅sγ+1)−(αb⋅s+β)⋅c​γ​sγ−1(c⋅sγ+1)2\frac{\partial t}{\partial s}=N\frac{\alpha_{b}(c\cdot s^{\gamma}+1)-(\alpha_{b}\cdot s+\beta)\cdot c\gamma s^{\gamma-1}}{(c\cdot s^{\gamma}+1)^{2}}

(9)


It is zero when the numerator is zero, which can be written as




(1−γ)​αb⋅c​sγ−c⋅β⋅γ​sγ−1+αb(1-\gamma)\alpha_{b}\cdot cs^{\gamma}-c\cdot\beta\cdot\gamma s^{\gamma-1}+\alpha_{b}

(10)


Let K=(1−γ)⋅cK=(1-\gamma)\cdot c, L=c⋅β⋅γL=c\cdot\beta\cdot\gamma, we can rewrite the expression above in the following form:




δ=K​αb⋅sγ−L​sγ−1+αb\delta=K\alpha_{b}\cdot s^{\gamma}-Ls^{\gamma-1}+\alpha_{b}

(11)


The optimal speculation length so​p​ts_{opt} needs to satisfy δ=0\delta=0.




K​αb⋅sγ−L​sγ−1+αb=0K\alpha_{b}\cdot s^{\gamma}-Ls^{\gamma-1}+\alpha_{b}=0

(12)


Since K⋅sγ>0K\cdot s^{\gamma}>0, L​sγ−1Ls^{\gamma-1} is a constant regarding bb, and αb\alpha_{b} is increasing with bb, δ\delta is monotonically increasing with respect to bb. Similarly, because K⋅αb>0K\cdot\alpha_{b}>0 and γ−1<0\gamma-1<0, δ\delta is also increasing with ss. Therefore, for a larger bb, so​p​ts_{opt} needs to be smaller in order to keep the δ\delta as zero, and vice versa, i.e., for a smaller b, so​p​ts_{opt} needs to be larger.






4 Adaptive Speculative Decoding: Our Approach




In real-world serving scenarios, the traffic might be time-varying, leading to varying batch sizes. Based on the observation and analysis that the optimal speculation length depends on the batch size, we propose a new adaptive speculation mechanism to choose the optimal speculation length under different scenarios.




The key point is to find the optimal speculation step so​p​ts_{opt} for each different batch size bb. While it is hard to find a closed-form solution for it, we can empirically measure the and do a grid search to find so​p​ts_{opt}. We divide the process into two stages, namely profiling and execution. In the profiling stage, we use a small sample of the dataset (similar to the training set in machine learning) to measure the latency under different batch sizes using different speculation lengths. Using the profiling result, we can build a look-up table (LUT) that stores the optimal speculation length for each batch size. During the execution, after a batch of requests arrives, we can find the optimal speculation length using the LUT, and configure the LLM execution, accordingly.




The overhead of profiling is negligible in LLM serving scenarios for two key reasons. First, we enable a very small search space. The optimal speculation length is usually small (less than ten). While profiling all possible batch sizes can be prohibitive. Instead, we sample only a subset of them. We profile batch sizes which are powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, …). For batch sizes that are not profiled, we choose the smaller speculation length of the nearest two profiled batch sizes. Second, the profiling overhead can be amortized, because LLM serving is usually a long-running serving task. A service can be online for weeks or months serving millions or even billions of user requests, while profiling only takes several minutes and it is only done once: before launching the LLM inference process in the server.




5 Evaluation




We evaluate the performance benefits of our proposed adaptive batched speculative mechanism using the methodology presented in Section 5.1 in two aspects: (i) quantifying a uniform traffic, where user requests are served by LLM at a fixed batch size (Section 5.2), and (ii) quantifying a dynamic traffic, where user requests are served by LLM at a time variable batch size (Section 5.3).



5.1 Methodology


Dataset.




We use the Chatbot Instruction Prompts dataset (Palla, 2023) from Huggingface. We only use the prompt field of it as the input.



Hardware and Software.




We use NVIDIA RTX 3090 as our benchmark platform. We use Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 11.8, and PyTorch 2.0.1.



Models.




We use OPT-6.7B (Zhang et al., 2022) as our large language model (LLM) and OPT-125M as the small speculative model (SSM).





5.2 Uniform Traffic




In this section, we assume that user requests are served by LLM with a fixed batch size. We compare our approach, i.e., adaptive speculation decoding, that integrates using the optimal speculation length, over the baseline LLM serving without speculation decoding. We sample 1000 prompts from the dataset and group them into batches. For each prompt, we generate 128 new tokens. Figure 4 presents the end-to-end time of finishing all prompts, including the tokenizer, by normalizing the results over the baseline without speculation decoding. We did a grid search to find the optimal speculation length.


Figure 4: Normalized latency with fixed batch sizes. 




We make two observations. First, adaptive speculative decoding provides higher performance benefits for smaller batch sizes. For example, when the batch size is 1, adaptive speculating decoding achieves a 2.73×\times speedup (63% latency reduction), while when the batch size is 32, the speedup is 1.31×\times. This is because when batch size is small GPUs are highly underutilized, and it is leveraged by speculative decoding. When batch size is large, GPUs are well utilized, so the room for performance improvement is limited. Second, across all batch sizes, adaptive speculative decoding provides a high speedup by on average of 1.94×\times over LLM serving with no speculative decoding.




5.3 Dynamic Traffic




In this section, we measure the effectiveness of adaptive speculative decoding in a real-world scenario, where the traffic highly varies over time. We create a server-client setting, and we artificially vary the number of requests sent to the LLM server per second.







(a) cv=0.5



(b) cv=1




(c) cv=2



(d) cv=5

Figure 5: Average latency with various traffic scenarios, i.e., varying request intervals and coefficient of variation (CV).











Figure 6: Timeline of four speculation strategies. Each point represents a group of 40 requests. The X-axis is the time stamp of the first request in a group. The Y-axis is the average latency of all requests in a group of requests. There is no optimal speculation length for all scenarios. When the request traffic is intense (e.g. 100-150, 200-250), a smaller speculation length like 2 is preferred. When the request traffic is sparse (e.g. 150-200, 250-300), a larger speculation length like 4 is preferred. Nevertheless, adaptive speculation decoding can always achieve performance on par with or better than both fixed speculation length schemes.


Client Configuration.




We launch a client process that samples a sequence of requests from the dataset and sends them to the server at a fixed interval time. The interval time is sampled from a Gamma distribution, and the parameters of the Gamma distribution allow us to control the average interval between requests as well as the coefficient of variation (CV). This way we can control the overall volume of traffic by varying the average interval, and the variation and blast of the traffic by varying the CV.



Server Configuration.




We launch a server process and wrap the LLM inference as a service that receives requests from a message queue and responds to the generated tokens via another message queue. If there is more than one request in the queue, they will be merged as one batched request (up to a maximal batch size of 16 due to the memory constraint).



Comparison Points.




We compare our proposed adaptive speculative decoding scheme with three schemes: 1) Batched LLM inference without speculative decoding, 2) Batched LLM inference with speculative decoding of fixed speculation length equal to 2, and 3) Batched LLM inference with speculative decoding of fixed speculation length. For fixed speculative decoding schemes, we select speculation lengths of 2 and 4, since they achieve better performance. We do not evaluate the speculative decoding scheme without batching, because it performs significantly worse than our remaining evaluated schemes.



Experiments.




We create dynamic request traffic on the client side and evaluate various volume and blast traffic configurations using four different values for CV (0.5, 1, 2, and 5) and eight different values for the interval time from 0.1s up to 0.8s with a step of 0.1s. For each setting, we generate only one sequence of requests, which is used to evaluate all comparison points. Each ’sequence’ contains 1000 prompts, and there are no overlaps between the dataset used in the profiling step of our proposed scheme and the dataset used in our dynamic traffic evaluation. We record the time tat_{a} at which each request is sent by the client to the server and the time tbt_{b} at which the server finishes serving the request and measure the latency as the difference tb−tat_{b}-t_{a}. Note that if the server is slow, requests cannot be processed in time and have to wait in a queue, thus the waiting time is also accounted for in the latency. Figure 5 presents the average latency across all requests achieved by all comparison points using different configurations for dynamic traffic generation.




We draw two findings. First, adaptive speculative decoding can provide high latency benefits in all various scenarios, including intense (low request interval) and sparse (high request interval) traffic, as well as uniform (low CV) and skewed (high CV) traffic scenarios. On average, adaptive speculative decoding achieves a speedup of 2.3×\times over LLM serving with no speculative decoding. Second, we observe that the best-performing speculation length varies across different traffic scenarios, i.e., there is no speculation length value that provides the lowest latency across all traffic scenarios. For example, when having CV=2 and a request interval equal to 0.1, a speculation length of 2 achieves the best latency, while when having CV=2 and and request interval equal to 0.6, a speculation length of 4 achieves the best latency. We observe that our proposed scheme effectively adapts the speculation length to the characteristics of the current traffic and achieves the best performance, outperforming both fixed speculation decoding schemes. Especially when the variation of the traffic is large (e.g. when CV is equal to 5), because the batch size might vary with the traffic volume, adaptive speculative decoding provides an additional 1.07×1.07\times average speedup over the better one of the two fixed speculation length.The speedup over fixed speculation length can be up to 1.15×\times.




Figure 6
presents the timeline on latency achieved by all schemes during runtime under time-varying traffic scenarios. In this experiment, the client alternates between two types of traffic: intense with a request interval of 0.2 seconds and sparse with a request interval of 1 second. The client will switch from one type of traffic to the other every 50 seconds. We fixed the CV as 1 in this experiment.




We find that adaptive speculation decoding effectively adapts to best-performing configuration. A speculation length of 4 performs better for sparse request traffic because the batch size is usually small, and a speculation length of 2 is more suitable for intense traffic. For example, from the 150th to 200th second, the traffic is sparse, therefore the speculation length of 4 performs better than the speculation length of 2. The situation is opposite from the 200th to 250th seconds. Nevertheless, adaptive speculation decoding can always match the performance of the better one of the two static baselines, or even perform better. Overall, adaptive improves latency over speculation lengths of 2 and 4 by 9% and 14%, respectively, on average. We conclude that our approach provides significant performance benefits by dynamically tuning itself based on the characteristics of the current traffic and leveraging the best of both speculative decoding and batching optimizations.






6 Conclusion




LLMs like GPT achieve significant success nowadays. However, LLM execution is inherently sequential, thus incurring low hardware utilization on GPUs. Batching and speculative decoding are two techniques to improve the GPU hardware utilization in LLM inference. To study the synergy between them, we carry out a comprehensive study, and observe that the optimal speculation length depends on the batch size as well as the characteristics of LLM model and GPU architecture. We build a quantitative model to explain this key observation, and based on our analysis, we propose an efficient adaptive speculative decoding strategy that selects the optimal speculation length for different batch sizes. Our evaluations show that our proposed method achieves equal or better performance than fixed speculation decoding schemes, and we hope our work will enable further research on accelerating LLM serving.

# C24 baseline timing diagnostic — AV off, k5

**Decision: `instrumentation_inconclusive`; adaptive verification remains unqualified.** Traffic, runtime identity and cleanup passed, but the timing evidence failed its predeclared adequacy checks. This is a limitation of our measurement, not an AV performance failure. Adaptive verification was never enabled, and no service speedup or full hypothesis A/B result is claimed. The user's two remaining full attempts are unchanged.

## Mechanism being qualified

The current server drafts five tokens, then runs the large target model to verify the proposed continuation. Adaptive verification keeps that five-token proposal but uses confidence and cost estimates to choose how many proposed tokens are worth verifying. Its potential benefit is fewer target-model token rows. Its costs include the controller itself, fewer accepted tokens per iteration, different graph shapes and extra draft padding. It needs a net improvement in time per accepted output token, not merely fewer target rows.

This differs from C03's occasional reduction of draft padding. C03 proved that its graph-selection mechanism activated, but never established a sufficiently expensive time contribution; its valid service screen failed promotion. Here the prerequisite is a direct, bounded observation of baseline target and draft work before selecting an AV experiment.

A concrete source-derived warning remains: with five real requests per rank, one valid adaptive dispatch changes target capacity **36→16 rows**, while draft capacity changes **35→80 rows**. These are reachable source-level capacities, not observed AV choices or predicted latency. The installed code already contains an AV controller and the checkpoint index contains its confidence-head weight; metadata presence is not proof of the head's runtime use. See [source feasibility and exact code chain](IMPLEMENTATION_FEASIBILITY.md).

## What ran

| Node | `jl-vm-541077`, eight H200s; this node only |
| Baseline profile | Original `latency-2xdep4-sla.yaml`, SHA256 `edb4c68cb4ee72415abe65c077683a8f88942bfcc8fff5833270ba05cdddcab8` |
| Runtime | Original pinned vLLM image, nominal revision `ac9126e58aa7bbab1856ba6593ba4d5003fea516`; installed file identities are authoritative |
| Model | DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, revision `2cba9e42aa026125f3ed06c6d98c1db82f7ca027` |
| Parallel layout | Two replicas, each TP1/DP4/EP4; two API processes per replica |
| Speculation | DSpark k5, probabilistic drafting, block rejection; **AV off** |
| Other baseline behavior | FP8 KV, prefix cache, Engram host offload and DP embedding; original graph capacities and request logging |
| Workload | First986 exact rows of the median Mooncake trace, ordinary runner at 0.5×; 299.232 s arrival span |
| Client | Original `.venv-aiperf`, seed 42, maximum 256 workers, 120 s warmup |
| Captures | Phase +90 s and +210 s; all eight workers; CPU+CUDA, warmup 1 / active 20 / max 20; no stack/shape/memory/FLOP recording |
| Observation | Three CPU `record_function` labels in two read-only source copies; removing labels reproduces original AST; no new synchronization or computation |
| Evaluator separation | Independent designer `c03_evaluator`; tooling builder `c03_evaluator_builder_review`; source/launch developer `c03_dev_review`; root owns runtime and publication |

The986-row prefix is a short sample, not the full 4,004-request workload. Its service score cannot be compared directly with C03's full-trace score. [Subset receipt](subset-receipt.json), [contract](EVALUATION_CONTRACT.md), [actual runtime identity](runtime-identity.json) and [capture inventory](startup-capture-inventory.json) bind the settings and sources.

## Workload and control validity

| Check | Observed result |
| --- | --- |
| Warmup | 55 completed, 0 errors |
| Profiling requests | 986/986 completed, 0 errors, 0 cancellations; unique IDs and workload keys |
| Completion ratio | 100% |
| Replay p99 / degraded | 4.6538368 ms / false |
| NOTICE versus exact phase start |NOTICE is 46,323 ns earlier; within the prospective 1 s bound |
| Four capture dispatch errors |+2.894ms,+4.844ms,+0.326ms,+0.713ms relative to exact phase+offset |
| Saved traces | 16 files, all eight workers in both episodes; no silent selection of favorable ranks |
| Final drain |Router and all eight running/waiting pairs zero for three consecutive 1 s samples |
| Original files and environments |All 30 pinned file checks and both package inventories unchanged |
| Cleanup |All eight GPU allocations released; ports 8000/8100/8101 closed; monitoring 9400 preserved |

The console's 107,615 ms replay warning exactly matches the **separate warmup** aggregate, not profiling. Both phase exports are retained. A server-metrics completion RPC timed out after the workload ended; its Parquet export later completed 3,105,464 rows and the client reported all results received. This is an observability delay, not a request failure or proof that every telemetry scrape succeeded. The runner exited 1 because the completed prefix missed service SLOs; service eligibility is not this diagnostic's fidelity gate. See [phase reconciliation](phase-final.json), [fidelity receipts](fidelity-builder.json), [cleanup](cleanup.json) and [integrity](final-integrity.json).

## Timing interpretation

The frozen criteria require at least ten complete decode-only cycles per rank/window, actual CPU-launch-to-CUDA correlations, both target and draft graph coverage, and at least 95% categorized device-busy union. The conditional materiality heuristic is target-attributed occupied time at least 20% of complete-cycle span on every rank in both windows. The adequacy gate failed before that heuristic could authorize any next experiment.

The decisive shortfall is replica 1, DP 2, phase +90 s: the trace contains 26 target ranges but only 8 native execute ranges, and only **4 complete eligible decode cycles** survive the required joins. Nineteen target candidates lack an unambiguous native/draft join, two are mixed prefill/no-generation, and one lacks its following boundary. Other rank/window cells retain 15–19 eligible cycles. A configuration requesting 20 active profiler steps did not guarantee20 readable decode cycles.

Five cells also contain GPU activities whose recorded end precedes the start of their supposedly correlated CPU launch:53,406,43,91 and54 events respectively. The reader retains them as unattributed and flags graph-coverage uncertainty. These observations do not distinguish a timestamp calibration problem from a correlation/trace-format problem; no invented correction or timestamp tolerance was applied. Their exact cause remains unresolved.

Readable cycle subsets show target-attributed occupied fractions of roughly 39.6–97.1% of cycle span. These are **descriptive values from an inadequately qualified capture**, not a validated AV opportunity or expected percentage saving. Some target-owned kernels are NCCL collectives, with individual long activities around 40–52 ms in replica 0's second episode. Execution or waiting inside a collective is not necessarily reducible by verifying fewer tokens. Uneven profiling/export across cooperating ranks is a plausible perturbation, not a measured causal explanation.

The predeclared inactive bracket at phase 110–130 s overlaps the first episode's replica 1 stop/export response until phase 113.651 s. It remains marked contaminated and is not shifted to a more favorable interval. The other three brackets have no control/export overlap. These brackets are descriptive context under different traffic, not an unbiased profiler-overhead estimate.

See the complete [reader output](trace-summary-v2.json), [trace inventory](trace-inventory-builder.json), [independent review](EVALUATOR_REVIEW.md), and per-cell timing table below. A cell passing local reader checks does not repair the required all 16-cell coverage.

Percentages use summed same-device complete-cycle span within each cell. Absence of observed GPU activity does not establish physical idleness, especially in flagged cells. Other/unattributed work and any overlap are retained in the [full table](timing-table.json) and [CSV](timing-table.csv); these columns are not an exhaustive additive partition. The required all-cell gate fails despite 11 cells passing local reader checks.

This heuristic does not establish a service critical path, reducible computation, an AV budget or expected speedup. Target ranges include graph-contained communication. Draft execution is a composite graph containing context preparation, model and sampling; draft execution is contained in draft proposal and must not be added to it again. Same-device unions and overlaps are required; summing ranks is not wall time.

## Consequence for the remaining attempts

Do not select AV as the highest-ROI experiment from this evidence and do not launch an AV-ON campaign. The source mechanism is still plausible, but we have not measured its removable cost. There is no automatic replacement run. Any further timing diagnostic needs a prospective instrumentation addendum addressing actual trace categories, timestamp associations, native decode-cycle coverage and rank-dependent profiling perturbation before consuming more GPU time. A later AV qualification must also measure its controller overhead, draft-padding tradeoff, accepted progress and correctness. No C03 patch is silently combined with it.

## Measurement issue preserved

Torch emitted CPU `user_annotation` and mirrored `gpu_user_annotation` events with identical names. The original reader selected by name alone and mixed CPU worker identities with the GPU namespace. The corrected, separately retained reader selects CPU annotation parents explicitly, then uses the same actual CUDA correlations. Independent review approved its two-line schema fix and ten CPU tests before the full 16-trace pass. The original reader/source and first-actual-trace reproduction are retained. No runtime rerun, different threshold or weaker attribution rule was used. [Offline schema addendum](READER_SCHEMA_ADDENDUM.md).

## Cost and preservation

Cold startup took about 26 minutes on this node, including about 20 minutes of model loading. The measured cause of that slow load is unknown. Task-owned containers occupied the node from 20:51:10 to approximately21:29:48 UTC: about 38.6 minutes, or 5.15 allocated GPU-hours across eight GPUs. This includes startup, warmup, replay, export and cleanup; it is not all active inference time. The arrival trace itself spans about 5 minutes. Future pilot budgets must include startup and evidence-processing costs.

All raw traces, backend/client/router logs, request exports and evaluator/source versions are preserved in the [checksummed evidence archive](../../evidence/av-k5-timing-001/README.md). Readable records are organized through [execution](../../records/EXECUTION.md), [analysis](../../records/ANALYSIS.md), [meta-learning](../../records/META_LEARNING.md) and the [C24 hypothesis card](../../hypotheses/C24.md). The original C03 execution artifacts and verdict remain unchanged.

claims.claim: The installed AV objective already includes draft and verification costs; adding a draft-cost term alone would duplicate existing functionality.
claims.conditions: The controller uses stale confidence products to estimate accepted tokens. Its denominator adds a draft cost indexed by request count to verification costs indexed by candidate token budget. Cost tables snap to profiled sizes within the capture range and interpolate above the configured limit.
claims.reported_result: Static implementation evidence: the chosen budget maximizes estimated accepted tokens divided by combined cost. No AV-on execution or performance result is supplied.
claims.transfer_inference: First check whether those table indices represent actual post-DP target and draft graph dispatch. Reuse C24 results when available; do not duplicate its pending timing. Any correction should address demonstrated cost-model error rather than introduce another controller.
claims.limitations: Calibration coverage, runtime confidence quality, actual dispatch and H200 gain are unknown. The draft term is constant across candidate budgets even though downstream draft padding can vary. C03 failed promotion according to the task; this source does not provide its measurements.

claims.quote: The same nominal k5 therefore does not imply unchanged draft execution cost when enabling AV.
claims.claim: Target-only AV savings can be offset by increased draft graph capacity through the existing DP synchronization contract.
claims.conditions: The supplied source analysis follows varlen target descriptors into FULL DP synchronization, then draft sizing by five times the synchronized request capacity. It assumes five real requests per rank and the original capture grid.
claims.reported_result: Source-derived counterfactual: fixed k5 selects target36/request-capacity6 and draft35/capacity7. AV with ten additional verified draft tokens can select target16/capacity16 and draft80/capacity16. These are capacity changes, not measured work or time. Even zero verification budget retains draft proposal work.
claims.transfer_inference: Cheap check: reconstruct zero, intermediate and full-budget dispatch from the captured descriptor rules, including cross-rank maximum padding. Future AV qualification must observe its own capture inventory and both graph descriptors. Compare accepted output against the complete critical path, accounting for overlap and synchronization.
claims.limitations: No AV-on run is reported. A new AV capture inventory can change the counterfactual. Actual target savings, draft penalties, rank imbalance and net H200 gain are unknown; C03 should not be recombined with this continuation.

claims.claim: Hopper FlashMLA provides a conditional AV eligibility path, but compatibility requires more than finding an SM90-capable attention kernel.
claims.conditions: The feasibility note reports ALWAYS variable-query graph support for the pinned compressed-cache and SWA builders, flattened query-token dispatch, and sparse FlashMLA eligibility on SM90. All current attention groups must satisfy the controller's query-length and FULL-graph requirements.
